operationalization: Code Mediterranean fishes for cyclic oral or pharyngeal reprocessing of food, using Sparisoma cretense as the scarus, and ask whether any other fish shows the same behavior. A second fish with cud-like rechewing would refute uniqueness; restriction of that behavior to the scarus would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: diet, food items and feeding type for Sparisoma cretense and other fishes, as a screen for herbivores that grind rather than swallow prey whole

obstacles: Chewing the cud must be mapped either to true regurgitation or to the parrotfish pharyngeal mill, and those readings can disagree.
FishBase records diet and teeth, not a rumination ethogram, so the behavioral criterion still has to be taken from papers.
rationale: The scarus is securely Sparisoma cretense, and FishBase covers its herbivory and that of other grinding fishes. Uniqueness is a universal negative, and the dataset does not record whether food is regurgitated and rechewed. The test can challenge uniqueness among well-studied taxa, not close it for fishes as a whole.

operationalization: Compare otolith and captive ages of Anguilla anguilla with a threshold of about seven to eight years. The claim is an existence statement, so any reliable ages in that range confirm it, and a maximum well below seven years would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity and life-history records for the European eel

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: published longevity and growth parameters for Anguilla anguilla

obstacles: The wording 'in some cases' is confirmed by a few old eels and is not a claim about typical or maximum age.
Captive maxima and wild otolith ages are not the same distribution.
rationale: Age of the European eel is a standard variable, and both AnAge and FishBase compile it. Because the claim only says that some eels reach seven or eight years, existing age samples can confirm it directly and would refute it if eels never approached that age. Longer lifespans do not contradict the wording.

operationalization: Treat hooked-talon birds as the raptor orders, and score each species' diet from plant versus vertebrate percentages. Any species with substantial seed or fruit use refutes 'carnivorous without exception'; a purely animal diet across the group would support that clause.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: species-level diet proportions for birds, to test whether every hooked-talon species is strictly carnivorous

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: beak and body measurements used with taxonomy to delimit the hooked-talon comparison set

obstacles: Diet percentages record what is eaten in nature, not whether a bird physically cannot swallow grain placed in the bill.
Parrots have hooked bills but not raptorial talons, so the group boundary needs an explicit rule.
rationale: EltonTraits gives diet fractions for essentially all birds, so the universal carnivory claim can be confirmed or refuted by a direct count of plant-eating exceptions. The further claim that these birds cannot swallow grain is a capacity test absent from the diet table. One documented non-carnivorous exception is enough to reject the statement as a whole.

operationalization: Score free-water drinking as present or absent for birds of prey, treating the kestrel and kite as the named exceptions. Repeated drinking by another raptor would refute 'never'; a systematic absence outside those exceptions would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts that sometimes record drinking, for a subset of kites, falcons and other raptors

obstacles: Drinking is rarely tabulated, so absence of a mention is not evidence that a species never drinks.
The claim is about a near-universal negative, which scattered anecdotes can refute but not establish.
rationale: Drinking is a clear behavior, but no open trait table records it. Species accounts and papers mention it for some raptors, which is enough to test the 'never' clause for those species only. A full test of birds of prey would require new, systematic observations.

operationalization: For oviparous vertebrates, score lung architecture as sac-like and poorly vascularized versus parabronchial and richly vascularized, and separately score drinking rate. A bird lung with a rich blood supply refutes the claim that every oviparous animal has a scantily blooded spongy lung.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT and mesh data for reptile and bird torsos that show lung form in a subset of oviparous vertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: digital anatomical slices used to compare lung structure across a few reptiles, birds and other amniotes

obstacles: Scans show gross lung shape better than how richly the tissue is supplied with blood.
Drinking rate is not in these anatomical archives, and 'all oviparous animals' includes birds as well as reptiles.
rationale: Lung type is measurable, and bird lungs are the obvious discriminating case against a single spongy, blood-poor lung for every egg-layer. Public scans and anatomical series cover only a subset of taxa and almost never quantify vascularity or drinking. The anatomical half can be tested for well-scanned species; the drinking half cannot.

operationalization: Among jag-toothed carnivorous mammals, compare plant eating in healthy versus clinically ill animals, and record whether the bout ends in vomiting. Regular grass eating by healthy dogs or wild carnivores would refute 'only when sick' and the purge explanation.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: plant versus vertebrate diet percentages for Carnivora, showing which supposed carnivores eat vegetation at all

obstacles: Diet percentages do not say whether the animal was ill or whether it vomited.
The purge story is a purpose claim; only the timing of grass eating relative to sickness is observable.
rationale: EltonTraits can show that many carnivores include plant matter, which already strains 'never eat grass'. It cannot tie those meals to illness or vomiting. Veterinary and behavioral papers on dogs fill part of that gap but are not a single open table, so the sickness clause is only partly testable.

operationalization: Compute dressing percentage as carcass or saleable flesh divided by live weight for domestic pigs, and compare relative fattening rate with other livestock of similar size. A dressing percentage far from five-sixths would refute that ratio; a match within ordinary breed variation would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service
candidate_datasets.role: live weight and dressed-weight statistics from livestock slaughter, for a modern estimate of the pig's flesh fraction

candidate_datasets.name: FAOSTAT
candidate_datasets.role: international livestock production and carcass statistics used to compare pig yields with other domestic species

obstacles: Modern dressed weight excludes different parts from Aristotle's 'flesh', and commercial breeds are not ancient Greek pigs.
Comparative fattening rate across 'any other animal' is much broader than slaughter statistics.
rationale: The five-sixths ratio is a direct dressing percentage, and slaughter statistics contain the two weights. Those series cover modern commercial pigs and a modern carcass definition, so they test a proxy for the ancient husbandry claim rather than the full comparative fattening statement. The ratio can still be accepted or rejected for present-day Sus scrofa domestica.

operationalization: Compare recorded longevities of Camelus dromedarius and Camelus bactrianus with a typical lifespan near thirty years and a maximum near one hundred. Records clustered around a few decades without any approach to a century would refute the hundred-year instances; ages near thirty would support the ordinary figure.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity records for dromedary and Bactrian camels

obstacles: 'About thirty years' is a vague central figure, while captive records are maxima rather than wild averages.
Failure to find a hundred-year camel is strong evidence against that instance, not a logical proof that none ever lived so long.
rationale: Camel longevity is tabulated in AnAge from zoo and husbandry records. Those records can check both the ordinary lifespan and the claimed century. Coverage is good for captive animals and thinner for free-ranging ones, but it is enough to accept or reject the extreme figure.

operationalization: Compare the honey bee's use of carrion or fermented substrates with that of other insects. Another insect that invariably avoids rotten food would refute uniqueness; regular use of rotten material by the honey bee would refute the bee clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI)
candidate_datasets.role: recorded feeding links for Apis mellifera and other insects, including some associations with decaying substrates

obstacles: Uniqueness across all insects cannot be read out of an incomplete interaction graph.
'Invariably' and 'rotten' are stricter than the presence of a nectar or pollen link.
rationale: GloBI and the entomological literature can show that the honey bee is a nectar and pollen feeder and that many insects are not saprophages. They cannot survey every insect for invariable avoidance of decay. The test works for well-recorded groups and leaves the universal 'only' open.

operationalization: Use breeding and wintering locations of Grus grus from the Pontic-Caspian steppe and ask whether those birds winter in the marshes at the headwaters of the Nile. Tracks or ringing recoveries ending there would support the route; wintering consistently elsewhere would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: GPS and satellite tracks of common cranes, for breeding areas on the steppe and winter destinations

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: seasonal occurrence of Grus grus from eastern Europe and western Asia through Africa

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence records used to compare the steppe breeding range with winter records near the Nile headwaters

obstacles: Modern flyways need not be identical to fourth-century routes.
The 'source of the Nile' has to be fixed as a geographic region before tracks can be scored.
rationale: Crane migration is now tracked, and occurrence data show where steppe populations winter. That is a direct test of a flight from Scythia to the marshes south of Egypt. Adequacy is short of the ancient period, but present-day routes are enough to confirm or reject the stated destination for the species Aristotle describes.

operationalization: Compare body mass or fat score of the same migratory populations at autumn departure from the breeding range and at spring return, with the common quail as the worked example. Higher autumn condition would support the claim; the reverse pattern in a well-sampled species would refute the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: EURING databank
candidate_datasets.role: ringing encounters and, where recorded, body mass of migrants including quail at seasonal passages

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: tracking studies that sometimes include body-condition measurements at departure and arrival

obstacles: Autumn and spring samples differ in age, sex and stopover, so mass is confounded with more than travel direction.
'All creatures' is far wider than the passerines and quail that ringing stations actually weigh.
rationale: Fat at the two ends of migration is measurable, and ringing and tracking archives hold masses for some species, especially the quail's general class of migrants. Coverage is seasonal and taxonomic rather than universal, and condition is confounded with breeding state. The quail clause can be examined; the claim about all migrants cannot.

operationalization: For hooked-talon birds, measure relative neck length and tongue flatness and code vocal mimicry as present or absent. A hooked-talon species that is long-necked or that does not mimic would weaken the joint rule; the rule would hold if those three traits co-occur.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: beak, tarsus, wing and tail measurements as a partial morphological frame; neck and tongue are not themselves columns

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of vocal mimicry and qualitative neck and tongue descriptions for raptors, owls and parrots

obstacles: No open table jointly records neck length, tongue shape and mimicry.
Aristotle's hooked-talon set mixes raptors with mimics such as parrots, which do not share talon morphology.
rationale: Each trait is measurable, but they live in different sources and mimicry is not a standard morphological variable. AVONET can support a restricted morphological comparison, and species accounts can score mimicry for many species. The three-part rule can be challenged for familiar families, not confirmed across every hooked-talon bird.

operationalization: Once the trichia is assigned to a modern clupeid or shad, test whether that fish moves from the Black Sea up the Danube and down a branch into the Adriatic. Occurrence on that path, plus a real river connection, would support the account; a drainage divide with no such fish movement would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence of candidate shads and sardines in the Black Sea, Danube and Adriatic

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: identities, distributions and migration notes for clupeid candidates of the trichia

candidate_datasets.name: HydroSHEDS
candidate_datasets.role: river networks and drainage divides, to test whether the Danube has a branch that reaches the Adriatic

obstacles: The trichia is not a secure modern species, and different clupeids give different distributions.
A hydrographic divide can refute a surface bifurcation without identifying the fish.
rationale: The route is a concrete migration hypothesis, and river networks plus fish occurrences can test it. The name is the limiting step: several sardines and shads are plausible, and they do not share one Danube-to-Adriatic path. Hydrography can reject a navigable bifurcation even while the species stays uncertain.

operationalization: Score dormancy in response to heat and to cold separately, using land snails, the purple murex and the scallop as the stated cases. Activity through the hottest season, or through winter, in a named case would refute that case; retreat in both extremes would support the general claim for that species.

candidate_datasets.name: COMBINE mammal trait database
candidate_datasets.role: hibernation and phenology flags for mammals, a subset of the animals said to hide from cold

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: life-history notes for muricid snails and scallops, including habitat and seasonal remarks

obstacles: Mammal hibernation tables do not cover snails, murex or scallops.
Aestivation of shellfish is described qualitatively and is not a downloaded seasonal activity series.
rationale: Heat and cold dormancy are real natural-history variables, and mammal hibernation is compiled. The claim's worked examples are molluscs, for which seasonal retreat is scattered through life-history notes rather than a trait column. The mammal half and a few shellfish can be examined; 'animals' as a class cannot.

operationalization: For snakes, lizards, geckos and the Nile crocodile, measure months without feeding and without surface activity in the cold season. About four months of aphagia in winter would support the claim; winter activity or feeding, especially in the crocodile, would refute it for that animal.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: month of occurrence as a proxy for winter activity of snakes, lizards and Crocodylus niloticus

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame and distribution for the named reptile groups

obstacles: Occurrence month is a proxy for activity, not a record of fasting.
Four months of hiding is latitude-dependent, so a single duration cannot fit both Greek snakes and the Nile crocodile.
rationale: Winter retreat and fasting are measurable, and seasonal occurrences can show that some reptiles remain active when Aristotle has them hidden. Fasting duration is not a column in these databases, so the 'eat nothing' clause depends on scattered herpetological studies. The crocodile in a mild winter is the clearest partial test.

operationalization: For the swallow, kite, stork, turtle-dove and the other named birds, compare winter locations with the breeding range. Wintering in sub-Saharan Africa or another distant region refutes hiding in local holes; recovery of marked birds in winter roosts on the breeding grounds would support concealment.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: migratory tracks of swallows, storks, kites and turtle-doves through the winter

candidate_datasets.name: EURING databank
candidate_datasets.role: ringing recoveries linking European breeding sites to winter locations

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: seasonal presence and absence of the named species on the breeding grounds

obstacles: A few individuals could still roost locally without making concealment the species' winter strategy.
Aristotle's list mixes long-distance migrants with birds whose winter behavior differs.
rationale: Tracking and ringing locate these birds in winter, which is exactly the contrast between migration and local hiding. Swallow tracks to Africa refute the claim that swallows pass the winter featherless in holes. The same archives cover the kite, stork and turtle-dove well enough to judge the list species by species.

operationalization: For female brown bears, record birth date, den-emergence date relative to the winter solstice, and whether they feed in the den. Birth in mid-winter and emergence about three months after the solstice, with no feeding, would support the claim; summer birth or regular den feeding would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length and life-history notes for Ursus arctos

candidate_datasets.name: COMBINE mammal trait database
candidate_datasets.role: hibernation and reproductive traits for bears

obstacles: Trait tables give gestation and a hibernation flag, not birth day, emergence day or den fasting.
Den studies are concentrated in a few monitored populations.
rationale: The three clauses are standard bear natural history and are measured in published den studies, but they are not columns in AnAge or COMBINE. A team can compile the timing for well-studied populations in weeks and leave other bear species and the strict 'eats nothing' claim less tightly covered. That is a partial test of a claim that is otherwise unambiguous.

operationalization: Count ecdyses across the life of crabs, spiny lobsters and clawed lobsters. A size series with more than one soft-shell moult confirms repeated shedding; a single terminal moult for those groups would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: growth and life-history records for commercial crabs, Homarus and palinurid lobsters

obstacles: Moult number is often inferred from growth stages rather than stored as a single count.
The claim is about the groups Aristotle names, not every crustacean species.
rationale: Repeated moulting is a direct life-history variable for the crabs and lobsters in view, and fisheries biology has published stage series for them. SeaLifeBase organizes those life histories. A small team can confirm multiple moults for the named groups without new fieldwork, which is enough to resolve the claim as stated.

operationalization: Compare documented multi-host or population-level disease outbreaks in fishes with the epidemic diseases of humans, horses and cattle. A fish epidemic with spreading mortality refutes the claim that no pestilential disease attacks fishes; only isolated individual illnesses would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: World Organisation for Animal Health
candidate_datasets.role: listed aquatic and terrestrial animal diseases and outbreak reporting, including epidemic fish pathogens

obstacles: Modern aquaculture surveillance is denser than ancient observations of wild sea fish.
Aristotle allows individual illness, so only spreading, population-level disease counts against him.
rationale: Epidemic fish disease is now a reported category, parallel to the livestock diseases he names. WOAH records include viral and bacterial outbreaks that kill many fish, which is the contrast the claim denies. Surveillance is biased toward farmed and managed stocks, but those outbreaks are enough to refute a universal absence.

operationalization: Expose Bolinus brandaris or Hexaplex trunculus to fresh water and record survival at one day, using occurrence in fully marine versus estuarine salinities as a weaker proxy. Death within a day would support the claim; survival well beyond a day at low salinity would refute the stated time.

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: occurrences of purple-dye murex species relative to the coast, as a proxy for avoidance of fresh water

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic identity and marine habitat of Bolinus brandaris and Hexaplex trunculus

obstacles: Distribution shows that these snails are marine, not that they die within a day of tasting fresh water.
The one-day lethality comes from scattered tolerance experiments, not a compiled survival table.
rationale: The one-day claim is a precise toxicity statement. Occurrence data can show that the purple murex does not live in rivers, which is only a proxy. Timed survival after fresh-water exposure is published piecemeal, so the numerical claim stays only partly testable.

operationalization: Identify 'measles' with muscle cysticerci visible in the flesh and under the tongue, then ask whether any non-pig host, and any suckling pig, carries the same lesions. Cysticerci in cattle, sheep or suckling pigs would refute the corresponding exclusivity; restriction to weaned pigs would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: World Organisation for Animal Health
candidate_datasets.role: listed cysticercosis of pigs and cattle, the modern diseases corresponding to flesh 'measles'

obstacles: 'Measles' is Aristotle's lesion name; cysticercosis is the historical identification, not a label he used.
Other skin pustules could be meant, and they would be scored differently.
rationale: If the pimples in the flesh are cysticerci, livestock-disease reports show the condition in more than the pig and can address age. That identification is standard but not certain, so the test resolves the parasitological reading rather than every possible skin disease. Suckling versus weaned status is less completely tabulated than host species.

operationalization: Use confirmed rabies cases after bites by rabid dogs, and compare fatality in humans with fatality in other mammals. Any human death from rabies refutes the exception for man; survival of a bitten non-human species that Aristotle would have counted would refute universal fatality outside man.

candidate_datasets.name: World Health Organization rabies topic
candidate_datasets.role: human rabies deaths and the transmission path from rabid dogs

candidate_datasets.name: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention rabies pages
candidate_datasets.role: case surveillance for human and animal rabies after bites

candidate_datasets.name: World Organisation for Animal Health
candidate_datasets.role: animal rabies occurrence across mammals

obstacles: Modern post-exposure treatment prevents some human deaths, so untreated outcome is the relevant comparison.
Reservoir species are not invariably killed by infection, which complicates 'any animal whatever'.
rationale: Rabies after a dog bite is a diagnosed, reported outcome in people and in other mammals. Human deaths directly contradict the claim that man is the exception who does not take the fatal disease. Surveillance is extensive enough, and the analysis is a straightforward comparison of reported cases.

operationalization: Rank the donkey against the horse and mule by lower critical temperature or cold-related mortality, and test historical absence on the Black Sea shore and in Scythia. Greater cold mortality in donkeys plus genuine ancient absence would support the claim; feral donkeys thriving in comparable climates, or ancient donkey remains in those regions, would weaken it.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: modern occurrence of Equus asinus, horses and mules relative to cold climates and the Black Sea

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: range accounts for wild asses and horses

obstacles: Modern absence can be husbandry rather than physiology, and ancient absence needs archaeological evidence.
A physiological ranking against the horse and mule is not a field in occurrence databases.
rationale: Occurrence data can map where donkeys live now, including cold regions, but they do not measure cold tolerance or fourth-century distribution. The causal link from intolerance to absence on the Euxine is confounded by transport and farming. The claim is only partly approachable with public biogeographic data.

operationalization: Score mortality of insects after external oil application, with a faster endpoint when the head is oiled in sun. Universal death would support the claim; survival of any oiled insect would refute 'without exception'.

candidate_datasets.name: ECOTOX Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: curated chemical toxicity tests, including oils and petroleum products, for a subset of aquatic and terrestrial invertebrates

obstacles: Toxicity tests cover pest and indicator species, not insects without exception.
Household oil smeared on the cuticle is not the same exposure as the mixtures in a toxicity archive.
rationale: The mortality claim is experimentally sharp, and oil toxicity has been measured for many insects in pest control and ecotoxicology. ECOTOX and the trial literature still omit most of the insect fauna, and protocols differ from Aristotle's smear-and-sun method. A counterexample would refute the universal, but the existing tests only sample pests.

operationalization: Map Holocene and ancient presence of lion and leopard in Libya, Asia Minor, Greece between the Achelous and the Nessus, and the rest of Europe. Lions in that Greek district and leopards absent from Europe would support the claim; European leopard records, or no Greek lions, in the relevant period would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil and archaeological-age occurrences of Panthera leo and Panthera pardus around the Mediterranean

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: historical and present range summaries for lion and leopard

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: modern and museum occurrences used as a check on European leopard and lion records

obstacles: 'More numerous' is a density claim, while fossils record presence.
Europe's boundary in the Caucasus and the date of extinction both change the scoring.
rationale: Presence of lions in the southern Balkans and of leopards in Anatolia is a historical-biogeographic question with fossil, archaeological and range data. Those sources are uneven in time and do not measure abundance. They can test presence and absence for the named regions and cannot settle 'more numerous'.

operationalization: Among mammal species pairs, predict viable hybridization from similarity of body mass and gestation length, holding phylogenetic distance aside as a rival. Pairs matched in size and gestation that never hybridize, or mismatched pairs that do, would weaken the rule; a positive association beyond relatedness would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length for mammal species used in the pairing rule

candidate_datasets.name: COMBINE mammal trait database
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass and reproductive traits for a taxonomically matched mammal list

obstacles: Hybrid records are scattered, and relatedness confounds size and gestation.
The Libyan watering-place story is not itself in these tables.
rationale: Size and gestation are compiled for thousands of mammals, so the predictors exist. Documented hybrids are not in one open matrix of comparable quality, and close relatives tend to share both traits and the ability to interbreed. The association can be explored and will stay confounded.

operationalization: Test wolf-dog and fox-dog ancestry with genome-wide markers and chromosome compatibility. Wolf ancestry in dogs, or fertile wolf-dog offspring, supports the first cross; no fox ancestry in Laconian-type dogs and no viable Vulpes-Canis hybrid would refute the second.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: public canid genomes and sequences for dog, wolf and fox ancestry tests

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: assembled dog, wolf and fox genomes used to compare ancestry and karyotype compatibility

obstacles: The ancient Laconian hound is not a living breed with a type specimen, so the fox cross is tested on dogs generally and on historical sighthounds.
Wolf-dog gene flow does not by itself prove the Cyrene anecdote.
rationale: Wolf-dog hybridization and the absence of fox-dog hybrids are genetic questions with public genomes. Admixture methods can confirm wolf ancestry in dogs and reject fox ancestry for the supposed Laconian cross. The particular Cyrene pairing is a local story; the biological possibility of the two crosses is what the data resolve.

operationalization: Regress known age, from otoliths or annuli, on scale size and scale hardness in scaly fishes. A tight relationship would support reading age from those two traits; wide overlap of size and hardness across ages would refute 'may be told'.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: growth parameters and age-length information for scaly commercial fishes

candidate_datasets.name: ICES
candidate_datasets.role: fisheries survey ages and lengths that show how well body and scale size predict age

obstacles: Age is routinely read from scale circuli, not from hardness, which is rarely measured.
Size-at-age overlap means size alone is a noisy proxy even when growth curves exist.
rationale: Fisheries archives pair age with length for many scaly species, and scale size tracks length. Hardness is not a stored variable, so half of Aristotle's criterion is missing. The analysis can show that size is informative but not sufficient to 'tell' age, which tests the claim only in part.

operationalization: Use sex differences in aggression or boldness as a proxy for 'spirit', and test whether females score lower in every gonochoric species except bears and leopards. A higher female score in another species would refute the universal; the reverse pattern in bears and leopards would be required to support the exceptions.
obstacles: 'Spirited' and 'courageous' have several behavioral translations, and they are not a trait-database field.
Published sex differences cover a small, biased set of vertebrates and are confounded by size and season.
rationale: A sex difference in aggressiveness can be defined, but it only partly matches Aristotle's spirit, and no public dataset scores it across animals. Existing ethological papers allow a check in a few mammals and birds, including the bear and leopard as special cases. The universal, and the claim that those two are the only exceptions, is not resolvable with what is compiled.

operationalization: Score agonistic interactions between species that share a site or a prey, and among conspecifics when food is experimentally or seasonally short. More fighting in shared-food pairs than in non-overlapping pairs would support the claim; peaceful coexistence on the same food, or no increase in fighting when food is short, would weaken it.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI)
candidate_datasets.role: recorded interspecific interactions, including some antagonistic and trophic links

obstacles: 'Enmity' can be read as a definition of competition, which makes the test circular.
Interaction archives record that a link exists, not how often animals fight when food runs short.
rationale: GloBI compiles biotic links, so shared prey and some antagonistic relationships can be counted. The archive does not measure fighting rates under food shortage, and many co-occurring species are not enemies in any observable sense. The claim can be probed as a statistical tendency and cannot be cleanly separated from the definition of competition.

operationalization: Treat supplemental feeding and long-term provisioning as a proxy for unlimited food, and measure approach distance to humans and rates of aggression among animals. Loss of fear and of fighting under sustained surplus would support the prediction; persistent wariness or aggression despite abundant food would refute it.
obstacles: No real setting supplies unlimited food, so experiments are proxies.
Tameness is confounded with individual habituation and with which species people choose to feed.
rationale: The sentence is a counterfactual about wild animals in general. Provisioning studies and a few classic fed populations, including Nile wildlife, record approach distance and aggression, but they are scattered and never match 'no lack of food'. They can reject the prediction for particular species and cannot establish it for animals at large.

operationalization: For known-age male Cervus elaphus, compare antler points with year of life through age six, and test whether point number still predicts age afterward. The stated sequence (none, spike, fork, three points, then no further age information) is confirmed by a match and refuted by systematic departures.
obstacles: Known-age antler series sit in wildlife-agency reports and papers, not in one open global table.
Nutrition and population change point number independently of age.
rationale: Point number by known age is exactly the wildlife measurement needed, and red deer have been aged from teeth while their antlers were counted. Those series are public but dispersed, and they vary by habitat, so they test the schedule for studied populations rather than for every stag. The 'after six years, antlers no longer indicate age' clause is part of the same comparison.

operationalization: At red-deer births, record whether the hind ingests the placenta before it reaches the ground. Consistent immediate swallowing would support the claim; placentas left on the ground or not eaten would refute the universal 'at once'.
obstacles: Placentophagia is described in ungulate natural history but is not a downloaded behavioral dataset.
Births are rarely observed closely enough to score 'before it falls'.
rationale: The behavior is specific and has been reported for deer and other ungulates, so published observations can support or challenge it for watched births. There is no systematic open dataset of hind parturitions. The claim is testable for a handful of observed births and not for hinds in general.

operationalization: For dogs, compare grass eating and subsequent vomiting in animals scored as ill versus healthy. Grass eating restricted to illness and followed by vomiting would support self-treatment; routine eating by healthy dogs without vomiting would refute that reading.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: plant fraction of canid diets, showing that dogs and wild canids eat plant matter, without health context

obstacles: Self-medication is an intention; the data can show only health state, grass eating and vomiting.
The dittany story about Cretan goats is a separate anecdote and is not in these tables.
rationale: Dog grass-eating has been quantified in behavioral studies, which can separate healthy from ill animals and record vomiting. EltonTraits only shows that canids eat plants. The observable pattern is partly testable; calling it treatment of an ailment adds a purpose that the counts do not decide.

operationalization: Watch gaping Nile crocodiles and score whether a small bird enters the mouth, takes material from the teeth, and leaves unharmed. Repeated entries of that kind would support the claim; systematic observation without them would refute it as a normal behavior.
obstacles: The trochilus has been guessed to be the Egyptian plover, but the identification is not secure.
Co-occurrence of crocodiles and shorebirds does not record tooth-cleaning.
rationale: The behavior is observable in principle and would be decisive if filmed at scale. What exists is anecdote and a long argument that the behavior has not been reliably seen. No public dataset contains mouth-entry events, so the claim cannot be resolved without new observation.

operationalization: Follow marked pairs of domestic pigeons, ring-doves and turtle-doves across years and record whether the pair bond ends only at death, allowing the occasional extra-pair mating Aristotle notes. Divorce of both living partners would refute strict pairing for life; bonds broken only by death would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: compiled mating-system accounts for Columba and Streptopelia, including pair-bond duration

candidate_datasets.name: EURING databank
candidate_datasets.role: mark-recapture of pigeons and doves, a frame for pair studies rather than a pair-bond table

obstacles: Ringing archives do not store mate identity.
Domestic pigeons, ring-doves and turtle-doves do not share one mating system.
rationale: Pair fidelity is routinely measured in pigeon and dove studies, and species accounts summarize it. The raw mate histories are study-specific, so a team can test familiar species and not every bird Aristotle grouped as a pigeon. Occasional extra-pair mating is already built into the claim and should not be scored as a refutation by itself.

operationalization: Classify nests of quails, partridges and similar heavy ground birds as constructed nests versus ground scrapes. A scrape on level ground would support Aristotle's description; an elevated or woven nest in those species would refute 'build no nests'.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: nest-site and nest-structure descriptions for quails, partridges and other galliforms

obstacles: A scrape can be counted as a nest, so the contrast depends on defining 'build'.
The purpose clause, that a nest would be useless to a poor flier, is not tested by nest structure alone.
rationale: Nest form for quails and partridges is described in standard species accounts and is a ground scrape rather than a constructed nest. That resolves the structural claim for those birds. The further claim that nest building would be useless because they fly poorly is a functional gloss that nest descriptions do not test, and similar galliforms are only partly compiled.

operationalization: When a person approaches a partridge or quail brood, score injury-feigning, the direction of the display away from the chicks, and the return call. A stereotyped distraction display would support the claim; flushing without feigning, in the same circumstances, would refute it as a general rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: behavioral accounts of injury-feigning and brood defense in partridges and quails

obstacles: The display is well described qualitatively and rarely stored as an ethogram dataset.
Quails and partridges may not share the behavior to the same degree.
rationale: Distraction displays are a standard, scored behavior, and handbooks record them for partridges. The evidence is narrative and video rather than a reusable table of trials, so the claim can be checked for the best-known species and not quantified across all broods. It is a partial but genuine test.

operationalization: Code palmation of the feet from taxonomy and handbooks, then test whether every web-footed species' habitat or occurrences fall by sea, river or pool. A web-footed species whose range is consistently away from water would refute the universal; universal association with water would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: habitat and geographic attributes for all birds, joined to a coding of webbed feet

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: foraging stratum, including water-surface and pelagic categories

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: occurrences used to check whether web-footed species are recorded away from water

obstacles: Foot webbing is not a column in AVONET and has to be coded by family.
'Near water' is broad, so only strongly terrestrial web-footed species would count as exceptions.
rationale: Habitat and occurrence are compiled for all birds, and the web-footed orders are a known set. Joining those two is a standard analysis that can confirm or refute a universal association with water. The purpose clause about structure is not separately tested, but the distributional claim is.

operationalization: Compare vocal rates of swans in ordinary life with rates in animals known to be dying, and check whether dying birds fly out to sea to sing. Song throughout life, with no concentration at death, would refute 'chiefly at the approach of death'.

candidate_datasets.name: Macaulay Library
candidate_datasets.role: recordings of living whooper, trumpeter and mute swans, showing whether song is confined to dying birds

obstacles: Archives are not linked to the singer's imminent death, so they cannot directly measure 'chiefly'.
Mute swans and northern swans differ so much in voice that the species Aristotle meant matters.
rationale: Routine recordings of healthy swans can show that some species sing in ordinary life, which cuts against song being chiefly a death behavior. They do not sample dying birds, and the flight out to sea is unmeasured. The claim is only weakly and partially testable.

operationalization: For Cuculus canorus, record whether it builds a nest, how many eggs it lays in each host nest, and whether the host incubates and rears the young. One egg per host nest, no nest of its own, and host rearing would support the claim; a cuckoo nest or regular multi-egg clutches in one nest would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Avian brood parasite-host relationships
candidate_datasets.role: compiled parasite-host list, including the common cuckoo and the hosts that rear its young

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: breeding accounts of clutch size per host nest and absence of a cuckoo nest

obstacles: 'Lays only one egg' can be misread as one egg per season; the test uses one egg in a given host nest, which is what the passage describes.
Host lists include occasional hosts, so frequency matters as well as possibility.
rationale: Brood parasitism of the common cuckoo is compiled as host relationships and breeding details, including the lack of a nest and the host's role in rearing. Those data can confirm or qualify the one-egg-per-nest description directly. The analysis is a tabulation of existing host records, not new fieldwork.

operationalization: Compare escape distance and nest defense of the common cuckoo with those of nesting birds of similar size. Exceptional timidity would match the stated mechanism; ordinary boldness would weaken it. The comparison still would not show that cowardice is why the bird parasitizes nests.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: qualitative accounts of cuckoo parental care and response to disturbance, set beside host behavior

obstacles: Awareness of one's own cowardice is not an observation distinct from the absence of parental care.
Low nest defense is a consequence of parasitism as much as a cause, so the test is confounded.
rationale: The observable residue of the cowardice explanation is that cuckoos defend young less than nesting birds. That difference is described, but it does not distinguish cowardice from other reasons for brood parasitism, including the loss of parental care itself. The mental-state wording has no separate measurement.

operationalization: Measure eagle home-range size, natal dispersal of fledged young, and whether other birds settle inside the territory. Large exclusive ranges and expulsion of young would support the maintenance claim; small overlapping ranges, or tolerance of neighboring birds, would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: GPS ranges of breeding eagles and dispersal of their young

obstacles: Tracks show space use, not active expulsion of other species.
Eagle species differ, and Aristotle's eagle is not a single modern species.
rationale: Home range and juvenile departure are measured for several eagles and can test the need for a large area. Interspecific exclusion of 'other birds' is a stronger claim than conspecific territoriality and is not what the tracks record. The spatial half is testable; the expulsion mechanism is only partly so.

operationalization: At sea-eagle nests before fledging, record whether adults orient chicks toward the sun, strike those that look away, and kill chicks whose eyes water. Repeated sequences of that kind would support the claim; nests without them would refute it as a normal practice.
obstacles: The sea-eagle may be the white-tailed eagle or another large eagle, but the behavior is undescribed for either.
Nest videos that exist were not collected to score this ordeal, and they do not amount to a dataset.
rationale: The ordeal is a specific behavioral sequence and could be confirmed or refuted by nest observation. It is not present in tracking archives, trait tables or a compiled ethogram. Resolving it requires new or purposefully reviewed nest records that do not yet exist as data.

operationalization: Describe the illicium and esca of Lophius and test whether prey approach the lure and are taken while the fish is buried. A lure that is anatomically present and attracts fish would support the claim; absence of the filaments, or no attraction, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: morphology and feeding accounts for Lophius spp., including the angling apparatus

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: specimen imagery of anglerfish heads for the filaments in front of the eyes

obstacles: Attraction of prey is behavioral, whereas most open records are morphological.
Several Lophius species fit 'fishing-frog', and lure use should be checked for the Mediterranean species.
rationale: The filaments and their use as bait are standard anglerfish biology, documented in FishBase and in anatomical specimens, with prey approach described in the fisheries literature. A team can confirm both the structure and the feeding sequence from existing sources. Species identity within Lophius is a minor ambiguity, not a barrier.

operationalization: Measure electric-organ discharge of Torpedo during prey capture and during contact with people, and record whether prey are immobilized. Discharge that stuns prey and is felt by humans would support the claim; prey capture without a shock, or no effect on people, would refute the corresponding part.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts and literature links for electric rays of the genus Torpedo, including the shock and its use in feeding

obstacles: Quantitative discharge traces live in physiology papers more than in a single fisheries table.
Several Mediterranean torpedo rays fit the name.
rationale: The shock, its organ, and prey immobilization are measured properties of electric rays, and FishBase points to the species and the literature that report them. Human numbness is likewise recorded. The data are more scattered than a trait column, but they are public and sufficient for a direct confirmation or refutation.

operationalization: For Silurus aristotelis, record which sex remains with the eggs, whether small fish are driven off, and the days until the young leave. Male care lasting about forty to fifty days would support the claim; female-only care, no guarding, or a very different duration would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproduction and parental-care notes for Aristotle's catfish

obstacles: Guarding duration is in species studies, not a FishBase numeric field.
The sheat-fish has sometimes been confused with Silurus glanis, which does not show the same care.
rationale: Male guarding and its duration are concrete and have been re-observed for Silurus aristotelis. FishBase records parental care only in summary, so the forty-to-fifty-day figure has to be taken from the primary studies. The behavior can be checked for this species and is not a general fish dataset.

operationalization: Classify Mediterranean fishes by diet as carnivorous or not, check the grey mullet, saupe, red mullet and chalcis as the named exceptions, and compare a movement metric between carnivores and the others. Further herbivores or detritivores would refute 'all except a few'; greater ranging by carnivores would support the second clause.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: diet and food items for Mediterranean fishes, including mullets, saupe and red mullet

obstacles: 'Wander most' is not a standard FishBase column and is only loosely matched by migration or depth range.
The chalcis is not a single secure species.
rationale: FishBase diets cover the fauna Aristotle is discussing and can accept or reject the short list of non-carnivores. That universal is the main clause and is directly testable. The claim that carnivores wander most is less cleanly measured, which lowers discriminating power without blocking a decision on the diet statement.

operationalization: Compare ink release of Sepia, octopus and squid in threat trials with and without a pursuit or a need for cover. Ink used as a screen during escape in cuttlefish and also in squid or octopus would refute 'the sepia alone'; ink only as a startle in the latter two would support the contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: ecology notes on inking for cuttlefish, octopus and squid

obstacles: Concealment and fear are not separate observable causes when the animal is disturbed in both cases.
Inking experiments are study-specific and not a comparative dataset.
rationale: All three groups release ink when disturbed, and that fact is recorded. Experiments that try to separate a smoke screen from a startle response exist as papers, not as a table, and the two functions are hard to tell apart. The uniqueness claim is only weakly testable.

operationalization: Place Octopus vulgaris on backgrounds of known color and measure skin match while foraging and while alarmed. A spectral or pattern match in both contexts would support the claim; fixed color, or matching only in one context, would refute the corresponding part.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: species account of color change in Octopus vulgaris

obstacles: Quantitative match scores are in experimental papers and image supplements, not in a life-history database.
Laboratory backgrounds are simpler than the stones Aristotle names.
rationale: Color matching at rest and under threat is a measured cephalopod behavior, with public experimental records for Octopus vulgaris. SeaLifeBase only summarizes it. A team can adjudicate the claim from those studies for this species, which is a partial scope relative to octopuses in general and relative to a single downloaded trait.

operationalization: Compare age at death of Octopus vulgaris, especially females after spawning, with a one-year limit. Deaths before a year would support the rule; routine survival well past a year would refute 'does not live the year out'.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: longevity records for octopus and other cephalopods

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: life span and semelparous reproduction notes for Octopus vulgaris

obstacles: Aquaculture and captive ages can exceed wild ages.
The claim says 'as a rule', so a few older individuals do not refute it, whereas a typical life past a year would.
rationale: Octopus lifespan and post-spawning death are reported in AnAge and SeaLifeBase and in the growth studies they draw on. Those sources can show whether a year is the usual limit for Octopus vulgaris. Female decline after spawning is part of the same life-history record.

operationalization: Film Argonauta argo at the surface in a breeze and score whether the web between the arms is held as a sail and other arms are used as oars or rudders. That posture while making way would support the claim; a web used only as a shell cover, with no sailing, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic and ecological summary for Argonauta argo, including notes on the shell and surface behavior

obstacles: The sailing account rests on few observations and is not a behavioral dataset.
The thin web is also the shell-secreting arms, so structure and the sailing function must be scored separately.
rationale: Surface posture of the argonaut can be filmed and has been re-described in a small modern literature. SeaLifeBase identifies the animal and its shell but does not contain sailing trials. Existing observations can challenge the sail-and-oar story and are too sparse to count as a resolved dataset.

operationalization: Locate the origin of the silk thread in spiderlings and adults: external sloughing from the body surface, or secretion from abdominal silk glands through spinnerets. Glandular secretion would refute 'not from their interior as an excretion'; silk shed like bark with no glands would support Aristotle against Democritus.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: microCT of spider abdomens showing spinnerets, for a subset of species

obstacles: Histology of the silk glands, not external shape alone, decides secretion versus a surface slough.
Scans and sections cover a minority of spider families.
rationale: The dispute with Democritus is anatomical: where the thread comes from. Silk glands opening on the spinnerets are described and imaged for many spiders, which is enough to test the mechanism in those taxa. There is no comprehensive public histology table, so the result extends to spiders at large only by sampling well-studied families.

operationalization: Identify pollen in individual honey-bee loads or follow one trip and count plant species. A load or trip confined to one species supports the claim for that bout; any trip that switches flower species before return to the hive refutes 'never meddles with another flower'.

candidate_datasets.name: Pollen collection by honey bees and bumble bees
candidate_datasets.role: individual pollen-load morphotypes and a direct score of floral constancy for Apis mellifera

obstacles: One landscape and season can refute a universal 'never' but cannot prove constancy everywhere.
Colony-level mixed pollen does not by itself show that one bee switched flowers.
rationale: Individual pollen loads record whether a foraging trip stayed on one flower kind. A public constancy dataset does that for honey bees and can refute the strict 'never' if mixed loads occur, or support high constancy if they do not. Geographic coverage is limited, but a counterexample anywhere decides the universal wording.

operationalization: In honey-bee colonies, count queens killed by workers, the fate of extra queen cells, and whether colonies that retain several queens divide. Frequent execution of surplus queens would support the observable half; retention of most queens without division would refute 'kill most of their kings'.
obstacles: Aristotle's kings are queens, which is a naming step but a secure one.
The motive, fear that the hive will split, is not distinguished by the deaths alone.
rationale: Worker execution of surplus queens and destruction of queen cells are recorded in apicultural studies. Those studies are not gathered into one open event dataset, and they do not show that the bees act in order to prevent dismemberment of the hive. The killing can be counted for managed colonies; the purpose remains a gloss.

operationalization: After a honey-bee sting in elastic skin, dissect the detached apparatus and see whether the gut is torn out with the sting. Death with only the sting, venom sac and associated glands left behind would refute loss of the intestines; extrusion of the alimentary canal would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical scans of hymenopteran abdomens for the sting apparatus relative to the gut

obstacles: Most scans are not of a bee at the moment of autotomy, so the detached parts still come from dissections in papers.
Death after stinging is not universal across tissues, since the barb catches mainly in elastic skin.
rationale: Whether the intestine comes out with the sting is a dissection result, and the barb, venom sac and glands are standard honey-bee anatomy. Public scans show the apparatus but rarely the autotomy event itself. The morphological claim can be settled from existing anatomical descriptions for worker bees and is not a single downloaded table.

operationalization: Mark honey-bee workers by age and record whether young bees nurse inside the hive and older bees forage, and score hair wear in each group. The reverse of Aristotle's assignment, or greater wear on foragers, would refute the claim; indoor work by the old and outdoor work by the young would support it.
obstacles: Age-task data are in marked-cohort and RFID studies, not one canonical open table.
Hairiness changes with wear and task, so it is not an independent marker of age.
rationale: Temporal polyethism is measured by following known-age bees, and those studies are public and detailed enough to accept or reject the claim that the old stay in and the young forage. They are scattered across papers and supplements rather than held in one archive. A team can resolve the direction of the age schedule for Apis mellifera without new experiments, but only by compiling those studies.

operationalization: In measured wind, record what departing or returning bees carry and whether a stone is held as ballast. Stones carried only in high wind, with a steadying effect, would support the claim; no stones, or loads of pollen and resin independent of wind, would refute it.
obstacles: Foraging datasets record pollen and resin, not stones held for stability in wind.
Anecdotes of bees carrying small objects do not identify ballast.
rationale: The ballast behavior is easy to define and would show up in load surveys paired with wind speed. No such dataset exists, and the published notes are too few to confirm or refute the habit. A decision needs new, systematic observation of what bees carry in wind.

operationalization: Separate worker wasps from overwintering queens and compare their presence after the winter solstice, using survival of marked workers as the direct test. Disappearance and death of workers, with only queens alive underground in spring, would support the claim; marked workers alive the next year would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: seasonal occurrences of Vespula and Polistes as a proxy for the annual disappearance of workers

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: dated photographs that can separate large spring queens from workers

obstacles: Not being seen in winter is not the same as death.
Polistes and Vespula differ, and some tropical or invasive colonies do not follow a single temperate cycle.
rationale: The annual wasp colony is well described, and dated records show workers vanishing and queens reappearing in spring. That phenology is a proxy for the claim that workers die and only mothers overwinter. Marked survival, which would settle death itself, is limited to particular studies.

operationalization: Among lions that attack people or livestock, compare age and tooth damage with lions that take ordinary prey. Attacks concentrated in old, dentally disabled animals would support the claim; attacks by prime-aged lions with intact teeth would weaken it as the general rule.
obstacles: Man-eater reports are case studies, not a sampled comparison of age and dentition.
Livestock raiding has several causes besides broken teeth.
rationale: Age, broken canines and prey choice have been recorded for a few famous lion populations and can be set side by side. There is no public dataset that crosses dental pathology with human or cattle attacks across lions. The pattern can be inspected in those case studies and not confirmed as a rule.

operationalization: Trace the elephant airway to the tip of the trunk and record whether an animal submerged except for that tip continues to breathe. Nostrils at the tip and successful snorkeling would support the claim; mouth-only breathing, or inability to ventilate through the trunk, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: scans of elephant skulls and trunks showing the nasal passage opening at the trunk tip

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: species entries for Elephas maximus and Loxodonta africana as the taxonomic frame

obstacles: Anatomy shows the airway; prolonged swimming is behavioral and is less often measured than the anatomy.
Both living elephant species should be included.
rationale: The trunk is the nasal airway, and that anatomy is available in specimens and scans. Together with straightforward accounts of breathing while wading, it decides whether the elephant ventilates through the trunk when the tip is above water. The behavioral endurance claim is a little broader than the scans, but the mechanism Aristotle states is directly checkable.

operationalization: Among hens that have dominated a cock, score crowing, mounting, comb and tail growth, and spur development, and compare them with hens that have not. Masculinization confined to hens after such a fight would support the claim; the same changes without any fight, or no changes after dominance, would refute the stated cause.
obstacles: Hen masculinization is a known endocrine and ovarian condition, but it is not tied in data to winning a fight.
Case reports are not a cohort of hens followed through dominance reversals.
rationale: Crowing, comb change and small spurs in hens are documented veterinary outcomes, usually after ovarian disease rather than after defeating a cock. Nothing public links those traits to the fight Aristotle makes the cause. The phenotype can be checked; the triggering story cannot.

operationalization: Compare comb color, crowing and sexual behavior in cocks castrated as adults and as chicks with intact controls. Loss of those traits after adult castration, and failure to develop them after early castration, would support the claim; persistence of crowing, comb color or libido would refute the corresponding clause.
obstacles: Aristotle's cautery at the rump is not the same operation as surgical removal of the testes, though both are castration.
Poultry results are in the agricultural literature rather than one open trait table.
rationale: The effects of castration on comb, crow and libido are classical, quantified poultry findings and can confirm or refute those outcomes. They are dispersed in experimental reports rather than a database. The anatomical site he burns is a separate detail from the endocrine result and is the main reason the test is partial.

operationalization: Compare voice pitch, androgen-dependent body hair and male-pattern baldness in men castrated before puberty with intact men. A persistently high voice, missing later hair and no baldness would support the claim; adult voice change, male body hair or baldness in that group would refute the corresponding clause.
obstacles: Historical eunuch series and modern hypogonadism records are clinical, dispersed and often restricted.
Castration after puberty, which Aristotle also discusses nearby, is a different comparison from boyhood castration.
rationale: Voice, hair and baldness under prepubertal loss of testicular hormones are measured clinical outcomes, and published series of eunuchs and hypogonadal men address them. There is no open individual-level dataset a team can download. The physiological reading of the claim is partly testable from that literature.

operationalization: Castrate male deer before antler growth and again while in hard antler, then record whether antlers ever grow and whether existing antlers are shed or enlarged. No growth in the first group, and retained unshed antlers in the second, would support the claim; growth or a normal casting cycle after castration would refute it.
obstacles: The evidence is a set of classic experiments and later deer studies, not a reusable open dataset.
Species and the timing within the antler cycle change the outcome and must be matched to Aristotle's two cases.
rationale: Antler growth after castration is an experimental result that has been published for deer and matches the two cases in the claim. A team can adjudicate it from those reports. Because the data are small historical experiments rather than a compiled dataset, the resolution is real but partial in form.

operationalization: Join presence or absence of upper incisors with whether the species ruminates, for cattle, sheep, goats, deer and the mammals that have upper front teeth. Rumination restricted to animals without upper incisors, plus the few toothed exceptions Aristotle allows, would support the rule; a large set of non-ruminating toothless species, or many ruminants with a full upper incisor row, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: trophic categories for mammals, to separate grazers and browsers that ferment and rechew forage

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: dental formulas, including absence of upper incisors, in species accounts

obstacles: Dental formulas are written into species accounts and still have to be tabulated.
Camelids ruminate and do not match the cattle incisor pattern, which is the exception the claim partly allows.
rationale: Upper incisors and rumination are both standard mammal characters, available in diet tables and dental descriptions. Joining them for ungulates is a short compilation and can confirm or refute the association, including the exceptions with teeth in both jaws. Coverage is good for the familiar ruminants and thinner for obscure herbivores.

operationalization: Score seasonal plumage color and song for the blackbird and a broader set of birds. A blackbird that is black in one season and yellow in another, with a changed song, would support the example; year-round black plumage and a seasonally changing but not species-changing song would refute that example.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: plumage and song descriptions by age, sex and season, including Turdus merula

candidate_datasets.name: Macaulay Library
candidate_datasets.role: dated recordings and photographs of blackbird plumage and song

obstacles: 'Many birds' is a weak quantifier, so the named blackbird case carries the test.
Seasonal song and a full color change are different phenomena and should be scored separately.
rationale: Seasonal plumage and song are documented for many birds, and the blackbird example is specific enough to check in field guides, accounts and dated media. There is no single table of seasonal color change for all birds. The example can be resolved, and the vague 'many' remains a partial scope.

operationalization: Test whether the European robin and the common redstart are seasonal plumages of one bird, using morphology, genetics and the fact that both can be alive and identifiable in the same season. Stable species differences, or both forms present as separate individuals, would refute the transformation; birds that change from one plumage into the other would support it. Apply the same test to blackcap and garden warbler.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: separate morphological measurements for Erithacus rubecula and Phoenicurus phoenicurus

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: seasonal co-occurrence of robin and redstart as distinct species

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: sequences that keep robin and redstart, and blackcap and garden warbler, as separate lineages

obstacles: Aristotle's erithacus and redstart names need the usual modern identification before the test starts.
Seasonal migration can put one species out of view without any individual changing into the other.
rationale: Morphology, occurrence and DNA all treat the robin and the redstart as different birds that overlap in time rather than as two plumages of one bird. The same sources separate blackcap and garden warbler. The transformation claim is directly refutable or confirmable with data already in hand.

operationalization: Code dust-bathing, water-bathing or neither for galliforms and larks, for waterside birds, and for hooked-talon birds. Dust-bathing confined to ground birds, water-bathing in waterside birds, and neither in most raptors would support the claim; dust-bathing raptors or water-bathing as the rule in galliforms would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: comfort-behavior notes, including dusting and bathing, in species accounts

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: foraging stratum and habitat as a weak ecological frame, not a bathing record

obstacles: Bathing mode is described in accounts and is not a trait column.
Many birds do both, so 'take a water-bath' and 'take neither' need frequency, not a single anecdote.
rationale: Dusting and bathing are familiar comfort behaviors and are mentioned for the groups Aristotle names. They are not compiled as a variable beside habitat, so EltonTraits cannot decide them. A partial coding from species accounts can test the main contrasts and will miss frequency and exceptions.

operationalization: The claim ranks the final cause ahead of the moving cause as a principle of explanation in nature and in art. No measurement of animals would confirm or refute that priority, because every developmental outcome is compatible with treating purpose as the starting point of the account.
obstacles: Explanatory priority is a rule about causes, not a difference in observable outcomes.
rationale: Aristotle is stating which kind of cause comes first in the explanation of natural things. Datasets of form, function or development can describe animals and still leave this ranking untouched. The claim has no measurable consequence that distinguishes it from a rival order of explanation.

operationalization: Follow vertebral segmentation in embryos and ask whether vertebrae appear by somite patterning before any mechanical breaking of a solid rod, or only after the fetus is contorted. Segmented somites in a straight early embryo would refute Empedocles' breakage account; vertebrae arising only as fractures from contortion would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: eMouse Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: staged mouse embryo anatomy showing somites and the vertebral column before fetal contortion

obstacles: The mouse atlas covers one model species, not vertebrates in general.
The wider claim that animal characters are not incidental results of development is a philosophical universal beyond the backbone example.
rationale: The rejection of Empedocles is testable: vertebral segments are visible in staged embryos, and the mouse atlas shows them arising as somites rather than as breaks in a bent rod. That decides the example. The additional claim that characters in general are not developmental accidents is not settled by one organ system.

operationalization: Estimate parent-offspring resemblance and heritability for morphological and other characters, in humans and in other animals that reproduce from parents. Heritable transmission of parental characters would support the claim; offspring characters statistically independent of the parents, across studied traits, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal QTLdb
candidate_datasets.role: mapped loci at which parental genotypes are associated with offspring traits in livestock

candidate_datasets.name: Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals
candidate_datasets.role: catalog of inherited characters passing from parents to offspring across animal species

obstacles: The claim says 'certain characters', so environmental traits that do not run in families do not refute it.
QTL and Mendelian catalogs are richest for domestic animals and sparse for wild taxa.
rationale: Parent-offspring transmission of characters is the measurable content of 'like begets like'. Public genetic catalogs show parental variants determining offspring traits in humans' companion and livestock species and, by the same methods, in other animals. That is enough to confirm the general claim or, if resemblance were absent, to refute it. Coverage is incomplete taxonomically, but the mechanism is directly evidenced where pedigrees exist.

operationalization: Aristotle grants other animals locomotion and reserves intellect, in his sense of nous, to humans. Any animal performance on a cognitive task can be reclassified as perception or memory, which he does not deny, so the outcome does not decide the claim.
obstacles: Intellect here is a theoretical distinction, not a score on a comparative cognition test.
A behavioral definition would replace the claim rather than test it.
rationale: The sentence divides intellect from the power of self-movement, which Aristotle already attributes to other animals. No public dataset of problem solving or tool use distinguishes that intellect from the capacities he allows to animals. The claim stays conceptual.

operationalization: Test whether ventilation cycles are driven by oscillations of body heat, as against blood gases and pH. Breathing that tracks heat load and ceases when heat is balanced, independently of carbon dioxide, would support the claim; a primary chemical drive with heat as a secondary stimulus would refute heat-cooling alternation as the necessity behind breathing.

candidate_datasets.name: PhysioNet
candidate_datasets.role: simultaneous respiratory and temperature waveforms used as a partial window on heat versus ventilatory drive

obstacles: Innate heat is not a variable; only its proposed effect on airflow can be measured.
Panting in heat and the chemical control of breathing are easily confounded.
rationale: The observable prediction is that alternating heating and cooling necessitates the intake and outflow of air. Respiratory and thermal records, including those on PhysioNet, and classic blood-gas experiments can test that against chemical control. They do it for a subset of air-breathing vertebrates and do not capture Aristotle's heat as he conceived it, so the mechanism is only partly resolvable.

operationalization: Within ant species, score winged sexuals against wingless workers and record whether any caste flies. Both winged and permanently wingless adults in the same species would support the claim; ants that are all winged or all flightless would refute the split he uses.

candidate_datasets.name: AntWeb
candidate_datasets.role: specimen photographs and caste data showing winged queens and males beside wingless workers

obstacles: Workers and queens are castes, not separate species, which is the distinction Aristotle needs and which the data also record.
A few species have wingless queens, so the check should not treat every species as identical.
rationale: AntWeb documents winged reproductive ants and wingless workers across a global collection. That is a direct test of the empirical claim that some ants fly and others do not. Caste identity is labeled on the specimens, and the comparison can be finished with standard queries.
